content: McBurney's point refers to a specific anatomical location on the right side of the human abdomen. It is situated one-third of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the umbilicus. This point approximately corresponds to the most common location of the base of the appendix, where it is attached to the cecum. Additionally, the anterior cutaneous branch of the iliohypogastric nerve is located near McBurney's point. Deep tenderness at McBurney's point, known as McBurney's sign, is a clinical indicator of acute appendicitis. Another related clinical finding is rebound pain upon the release of applied pressure, which is referred to as Aaron's sign. When tenderness is specifically localized to McBurney's point, it suggests that the inflammation has progressed beyond the lumen of the bowel, which typically causes poorly localized pain, and is now irritating the peritoneal lining. This irritation occurs at the site where the peritoneum comes into contact with the inflamed appendix. The presence of tenderness at McBurney's point is indicative of the progression of acute appendicitis to a more advanced stage, increasing the likelihood of rupture. However, the anatomical position of the appendix can vary significantly among individuals and may migrate within the abdomen. For example, in cases of a retrocecal appendix (an appendix located behind the cecum), tenderness at McBurney's point may not be present. Consequently, many cases of appendicitis do not exhibit point tenderness at this location. It is also important to note that other abdominal conditions can sometimes cause tenderness at McBurney's point. Therefore, while this sign is highly useful in the clinical evaluation of appendicitis, it is neither a necessary nor a sufficient criterion for diagnosing acute appendicitis. The variability in the anatomical position of the appendix further limits the diagnostic utility of McBurney's sign.
